title: A million calls, a million cases and a target nobody put in writing
lede: Coca-Cola never published a sales figure for OK in a filing. What exists is one sentence from a spokesman, a target reported by newspapers, a few counts from the campaign and the company-wide advertising line in the 10-K.

blocks.title: Four figures, four kinds of source

items.text: **A spokesman’s figure.** Cases sold from introduction to September 1995, as given to The New York Times.[^9] The only sales number Coca-Cola ever gave.

**A press report of the target.** The Washington Post said OK’s purpose was to take 3 to 4% of a $50 billion soft drink market, which “would make it the most successful new soda in a dozen years.”[^8]
**A company claim.** Calls to the 800 line by early September 1994, “despite the limits of the test markets.”[^8]
**Mentions in Coca-Cola’s annual reports on Form 10-K:** the words “OK soda” in a list of products for 1994. None for 1993 or 1995.[^1][^2][^3]

blocks.title: Sixteen months in test
blocks.subtitle: Number of US test cities reported in the press. The count comes from two different publications and is not a company figure.

points.title: Zyman returns
points.text: Sergio Zyman rejoins Coca-Cola as chief marketing officer.[^1] No product yet.

points.title: announced
points.text: Introduced to the press on April 20; not yet on sale.[^4]

points.title: nine cities
points.text: Time’s count, “from Boston to Seattle,” with a national rollout planned for the summer.[^6]

points.title: eight cities
points.text: The Washington Post’s count, with “dismal sales” in Minneapolis.[^8] We do not know whether a city was dropped or the counts simply differ.

points.title: phased out
points.text: Withdrawn from “those test markets.”[^9] Plotted as zero; the date the last cans were sold is unknown.

blocks.source: Time, May 30, 1994[^6]; The Washington Post, Sep 3, 1994[^8]; The New York Times, Sep 13, 1995[^9]; Coca-Cola Form 10-K for 1994[^1]. The zeros are plotting conventions. Later lists of test markets name more places than nine; we could not trace them to a period source.

blocks.title: The share Coca-Cola wanted, and the brands on either side of it
blocks.subtitle: Percent of the US soft drink market in 1994, as stated in the press. OK’s own share was never published.

items.label: OK: reported target, upper end
items.note: “3 to 4 percent” in The Washington Post; 4% and $1 billion in The Believer’s later account.[^8][^13]

items.label: Mountain Dew (Pepsi)
items.note: The most popular soda aimed at teenagers, per Time.[^6]

items.label: Mello Yello (Coca-Cola)
items.note: Coke’s existing citrus brand, per Time.[^6]

blocks.source: Time, May 30, 1994[^6]; The Washington Post, Sep 3, 1994[^8]; The Believer, Feb 2014[^13]. The Post describes the $50 billion market as worldwide; the other sources describe a US share. Figures are shown side by side for scale only.

blocks.title: The gap OK was meant to close

left.label: Mountain Dew’s share of the US soft drink market, 1994[^6]

blocks.equation: 3.5 ÷ 0.3 ≈ 11.7, shown as 12 bottles. Both shares are from Time, May 30, 1994.[^6]

blocks.title: The budget it came out of
blocks.subtitle: The Coca-Cola Company’s advertising expenditures, all brands, worldwide. OK’s share of this was never disclosed.
blocks.source: The Coca-Cola Company, Form 10-K for 1994: “Advertising expenditures were $1,308 million in 1994, $1,126 million in 1993 and $1,107 million in 1992.”[^1] The increase from 1993 to 1994 is $182 million, or about 16% (derived). Nothing in the filing attributes any of it to OK.

blocks.title: What Coca-Cola told its shareholders
blocks.subtitle: The soft drink product list in three consecutive annual reports on Form 10-K.
rows: “…TAB, caffeine free TAB, OK soda, Fresca, PowerAde, Fruitopia…” TAB Clear is gone.[^1]
No OK. Fruitopia remains; Barq’s root beer is added.[^3]

blocks.caption: Small numbers from the test

rows.text: 12-packs a week, at most, at Byerly’s, a chain of nine Twin Cities supermarkets, plus about 20 liter bottles[^8]
12-packs sold at one Minneapolis-area SuperAmerica store, according to its manager[^8]
countries outside the United States where Coca-Cola said it planned to introduce OK[^8]
cases a month, roughly: one million cases over about 14 months (derived, and it depends on which start date you use)[^9]

blocks.source: The Washington Post, Sep 3, 1994[^8]; The New York Times, Sep 13, 1995.[^9]

blocks.body: Unknown, because Coca-Cola did not publish them: OK’s sales in dollars, its market share in any city, what was spent on advertising it, the size of a “case” in the spokesman’s figure, and any write-off. The Times item says the drink was introduced in July 1994; every 1994 source we read has it on sale in May.
